name: Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi
funding: Run by the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi; the pages read state no funder, cost or collection value, and its chairman said acquisition prices will likely never be revealed (The Art Newspaper, 2 Dec 2025).
watch: A 35,000 sq m museum by Mecanoo on Saadiyat Island, opened in November 2025. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism, said acquisition prices will likely never be revealed.
why_flagged: The Art Newspaper (2 Dec 2025) states the museum is run by Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism.
records_note: No accounts were found in the pages read.

overview: A natural history museum of 35,000 sq m in the Saadiyat Cultural District, designed by the Dutch firm Mecanoo (The Art Newspaper, 2 Dec 2025).
The opening ceremony was held on 21 November 2025 and it opened to the public the following Saturday (The National, 26 Nov 2025).

What is there: natural history from the formation of the universe through the age of dinosaurs to present biodiversity, with a focus on the Arabian region; Stan, an 11.7 m tall fossilised Tyrannosaurus rex, a seven-billion-year-old meteorite and a recreation of Abu Dhabi seven million years ago (The National, 26 Nov 2025). Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974, is on loan from the Ethiopian cultural authority (The Art Newspaper, 2 Dec 2025). Al Mubarak said most of the fossils are over 50 per cent real, not resin figures (The National, 23 Nov 2025).

Archive: the museum is being prepared as a research hub with partnerships in renewable energy, aviation, transportation, genetics and medical science; no library or archive is described (The National, 23 Nov 2025).
details.funding_verdict: Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi: state, run by the Abu Dhabi government's culture department; no cost published
funding: No cost, funder or collection value is stated in the pages read; Al Mubarak said: We don't like to be loud about things (The National, 23 Nov 2025).

red_flags.heading: Undisclosed acquisition prices
points: Al Mubarak told The National (23 Nov 2025) that acquisition prices will likely never be revealed. No reply from other parties was found.

details.bottom_line: A state museum opened in November 2025 with no published cost or acquisition prices. What to watch: whether the Department of Culture and Tourism ever states what it paid for Stan and the other specimens.
details.website: https://www.saadiyat.ae/enjoy/natural-history-museum-abu-dhabi (not opened; third-party visitor page, the museum's own site was not found)

name: Eskenazi Museum of Art
funding: The art museum of Indiana University, a public university. Sidney and Lois Eskenazi gave $15M in 2016 for the renovation and the name.
watch: Indiana University cancelled the Samia Halaby retrospective in December 2023. PEN America urged reinstatement and a petition drew 8,000 signatures.
why_flagged: The art museum of Indiana University, a public university. Sidney and Lois Eskenazi gave $15M in 2016 for the renovation and the name.
records_note: It posts annual reviews for 2020 to 2023. Parent Indiana University posts audited annual financial reports and names its nine trustees.
affiliations_note: The art museum of Indiana University Bloomington, which uses IU Auditorium for event booking and management.

overview: Art museum of Indiana University Bloomington, at 1133 East Seventh Street on the Bloomington campus.

Opened in 1941 as the Indiana University Museum of Art under Henry Radford Hope, in a gallery in Mitchell Hall. Renamed the Sidney and Lois Eskenazi Museum of Art in May 2016 (Wikipedia, museum news release).
Named for Sidney and Lois Eskenazi, Indianapolis-based philanthropists (museum news release).

The I.M. Pei and Partners building, dedicated in 1982, is two concrete triangles joined by a glass-roofed atrium. It closed in May 2017 for a renovation by Susan T. Rodriguez of Ennead Architects with Browning Day Mullins Dierdorf and reopened in November 2019 (Wikipedia, museum news release).

About 45,000 objects, including ancient jewellery and paintings by Picasso and Jackson Pollock, with a café and shop. Mindy N. Besaw was hired as director in 2025, after David A. Brenneman (from 2015) (Wikipedia).

Admission is free. Open Tuesday to Sunday, closed Monday. Thursdays to 7pm. Two lifts serve all galleries, wheelchairs can be borrowed, and there is a weekly sensory-friendly hour and ADA parking behind the building.
details.funding_verdict: Eskenazi Museum of Art: university-run: Indiana University, with private naming and renovation gifts
funding: Sidney and Lois Eskenazi gave $15 million in 2016, the largest cash gift in the museum's history, as the lead gift for the renovation, plus nearly 100 prints including 34 works by Miró; IU added $20 million through its bicentennial campaign match (museum news release).

red_flags.heading: University cancelled a Palestinian artist's retrospective
points: On 20 December 2023 Indiana University cancelled "Samia Halaby: Centers of Energy", the first US retrospective of the Palestinian artist and IU alumna, due to open on 10 February 2024 after three years of work; IU cited "concerns about guaranteeing the integrity of the exhibit for its duration" (Indiana Public Media, Hyperallergic).
Halaby said: "Clearly the intent is to suppress Palestinian voices at this very time" (The Art Newspaper).
In November 2023 US Representative Jim Banks had written to IU president Pamela Whitten about antisemitism on campus, calling pro-Palestinian protests "pro-terrorist" (Indiana Public Media).
Provost Rahul Shrivastav called the show a "lightning rod" for protests and said IU would "err on the side of caution" when there was a risk of violence (Indiana Public Media).

red_flags.heading: Protest over the cancellation
points: A petition by Halaby's grandniece Madison Gordon passed 13,500 signatures by 18 January 2024 (Indiana Public Media).

PEN America's Artists at Risk Connection called it "an alarming affront to free expression", and the National Coalition Against Censorship wrote to Whitten on 11 January 2024 (Indiana Public Media, Hyperallergic).
On 7 February 2024, 75 faculty and staff signed a letter criticising IU's lack of transparency; three artists withdrew from the Eskenazi School's McKinney Visiting Artist Series (Herald-Times).
The Broad Art Museum at Michigan State University hosted the retrospective in June 2024 (Wikipedia).

press.overall: Strong criticism in the art press, all about the 2023 Halaby cancellation; it targets the university's decision more than the museum's staff.

items.title: Elaine Velie, "Indiana University Cancels Palestinian Artist Samia Halaby's Exhibition" (2024)
points: Unverified: that the decision was tied to Halaby's pro-Palestine advocacy and social media, from Hyperallergic citing emails and a petition; the university cited concerns about the exhibit's integrity.
Quotes the petition: "the University is canceling the show to distance itself from the cause of Palestinian freedom."

items.title: Theo Belci, "US museum under fire for cancelling Palestinian artist's retrospective" (2024)
points: Reports the petition's claim that IU gave "no evidence of threats" to the artwork, the campus or Halaby.
Notes Halaby asked why the university did not speak up "during the three long years of preparation".

details.bottom_line: No funding controversy was found behind the museum: its university and an Indianapolis couple's naming gift. The weak point is the university's December 2023 cancellation of the Halaby retrospective, which PEN America called "an alarming affront to free expression" and which drew a petition, faculty protest and artist withdrawals. Worth watching: whether the new director restores the show or changes how such decisions are made.

name: New Orleans Museum of Art
funding: Expenses $13.1M (2024). Contributions 62%. Trustees include Gayle Benson and Walda Besthoff (retail). First Horizon Bank.
watch: Flag rests on the Helis Foundation (William Helis oil family), a current sponsor of free admission.
why_flagged: Non-funding row: #DismantleNOMA racism claims (2020) and the June 2023 backlash over a curator hire. The current donor roster is unpublished (last one is 2019).
records_note: NOMA posts annual reports for 2011 to 2020, financial statements for 2011 to 2021, a donor list inside the 2020 report and its 2026 trustees.
finances_note: FY2024 income USD 10.0M: about 6 percent government grants, 56 percent contributions, memberships and event gifts, 18 percent admissions and shop, 15 percent investment returns (Form 990, Part VIII).
affiliations_note: Includes the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden in City Park; its pages name no parent, network or partner institution. Member of AAMD.

overview: Art museum in City Park at One Collins C. Diboll Circle (Wikipedia).
Founded in 1911 with funding from the philanthropist Isaac Delgado, who died in January 1912. Opened on 11 December 1911 as the Delgado Museum of Art (Wikipedia).
Former city chief engineer Benjamin Morgan Harrod partly designed the building. A $23 million expansion opened in 1993 (Wikipedia).
The collection holds more than 40,000 objects spanning about 5,000 years. The 11.5 acre Besthoff Sculpture Garden has over 90 sculptures. Café NOMA by Ralph Brennan is on site (Wikipedia).

Visiting: museum open Tuesday to Sunday 10am to 5pm, Wednesdays noon to 7pm. The Sculpture Garden is free and open seven days (museum website). A 2023 museum press release gave adults $15 and children 12 and under free.
details.funding_verdict: New Orleans Museum of Art: privately funded: trustees, foundations and donors
funding: The Helis Foundation, "established and funded by the William Helis Family in 1955" (foundation website), sponsors NOMA's free days through its Art for All programme, which the foundation says began in 2007; Wednesdays became the free day on 3 March 2021 (foundation post, 8 March 2021). A NOMA release of 1 June 2023 credits it for free Wednesdays for Louisiana residents and free entry for ages 13 to 19.

red_flags.heading: Helis Foundation, oil family money
points: The foundation's post of 8 March 2021 calls William George Helis, whose family set up the foundation in 1955, five years after his death, an oil magnate. Its leader David Kerstein is described by the foundation as "a soft-spoken lawyer, oil-company executive and philanthropist". The foundation's about and Art for All pages do not mention oil.

The open letter of 12 October 2020 supporting #DismantleNOMA says the museum is sustained by "oil money and other harmful private funders" and cites the Helis Foundation, which it says funds museum events and subsidises free admission for teenagers (Hyperallergic, Hakim Bishara). Unverified: the letter's description of the foundation as the philanthropic arm of the Helis Oil & Gas Energy Project; no document in the piece shows it.

red_flags.heading: Open letters alleging racism, 2020
points: In June 2020 five former NOMA workers published an open letter saying 30 employees resigned in two years because of a "toxic work environment and institutional racism". It alleged slurs, wage discrimination against Black workers, surveillance, non-disclosure agreements and a permanent plantation parlor installation; NOMA declined to comment on specifics, citing "privacy restrictions" (Hyperallergic, Hakim Bishara, 25 June 2020).

A second letter on 12 October 2020, signed by more than 150 people including the Guerrilla Girls and Michael Rakowitz, demanded the removal of director Susan M. Taylor and an independent investigation, and urged artists to withhold labour and support. NOMA said it was "committed to being an anti-racist institution" (Hyperallergic, Hakim Bishara).

On 29 June 2023 NOMA announced Amanda Maples, a white woman, as curator of African art. More than 850 Instagram comments criticised the hire. NOMA announced a town hall, and on 30 June a spokesperson told Gambit her record led to her selection (The Art Newspaper, Torey Akers, 3 July 2023).

press.overall: Art media criticism concerns racism, workplace culture and hiring; funding appears in one line on oil money.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Open Letter Lambastes Racism and Homophobia at New Orleans Museum of Art" (2020)
points: Reports the former staff's allegations, listed above; NOMA declined to respond to specifics.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "150 Artists Amplify Demands for Reform at New Orleans Museum of Art" (2020)
points: Reports the letter's call to implement thirteen changes from #DismantleNOMA, including removing the director; the letter says the board "has largely remained silent", that the museum is sustained by oil money citing the Helis Foundation, and that founder Isaac Delgado's wealth "derives from a sugar plantation".

items.title: Torey Akers, "New Orleans Museum of Art faces public outcry for hiring white curator of African art" (2023)
points: Reports criticism from local journalist Megan Braden-Perry, arts worker Alexis Jackson and the nonprofit No White Saviors; ties it to tensions since 2020.
News report of criticism, not the paper's own critique.

details.bottom_line: The museum is privately funded and little donor detail is published. The clearest funding weak point is the Helis Foundation, set up by the family of an oil magnate and led by an oil-company executive. Watch for a current donor and trustee list.

name: Kharkiv Municipal Gallery
funding: Founded 1996 as Ukraine's first gallery with municipal status. The city council culture department decides on its premises.
watch: Upper halls closed since 2022 and its White Cube now serves the city's news studio. The ARTbasement, also a shelter, reopened in September 2023.
records_note: It names only co-founder and director Tatyana Tumasyan.

overview: Contemporary art gallery at Chernyshevska Street 15, Kharkiv, described by Wikipedia as one of the first Ukrainian galleries of contemporary art. It opened in 1996 and joined the Association of Art Galleries of Ukraine in 1997 (Wikipedia).

Spaces: a main exhibition hall of about 100 square metres and an underground space of about 140 square metres, the ARTbasement (ARTpidval), which has worked with youth and experimental art since 2008 (Wikipedia).

Programmes: the NonStopMedia youth projects festival since 2003, a curatorial intensive first held in 2015, Night of Museums in Kharkiv, Night of Performance since 2016, the retrospective series "Our Heritage" and residency exchanges since 2011 (Ukrainian Wikipedia).
Wikipedia lists Tetiana Tumasian as director and curator.

Wartime: Objectiv.tv reported on 11 March 2023 that the gallery had not operated since the full-scale war began, with six staff, two of them in Kharkiv. According to the report, the city council and Mayor Ihor Terekhov had agreed remotely with the director that the city's communal news programme "Харків: новини" would use the premises at Chernyshevska 15 temporarily, and staff were told they would move to a children's art school at Yesenina Street 8A. After public backlash, Terekhov phoned the director on 11 March and, according to the gallery, said the premises would remain gallery space, that the city guarantees its return, and that the collection, archive and library would stay in the sealed storage on site. The gallery said it was waiting for documented guarantees (Objectiv.tv, Olena Nahorna, "Переселення «муніципалки» заради комунального ТБ: що гарантує Терехов (відео)", 11 March 2023; title translated: relocation of the "municipal gallery" for communal TV: what Terekhov guarantees).
details.funding_verdict: Kharkiv Municipal Gallery: municipal: an institution of Kharkiv city
funding: Wikipedia describes it as a municipal gallery, and the 2023 Objectiv.tv report shows the city council and the mayor deciding how its premises are used.
details.bottom_line: The gallery is a city of Kharkiv institution, and the city council decides how its premises are used.

name: National History Museum
funding: A state institution under Albania's Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation. Its 2024 to 2028 reconstruction is funded by the state Public Investment programme (606 million lek) and EU4Culture.
watch: Albania's largest museum, opened 28 October 1981; a Communist Terror pavilion was added in 2012 and it closed in March 2024 for four years.

propaganda.summary: Hoxha's regime built the museum from 1978 and opened it in 1981 with displays shaped to the communist narrative and a socialist realist mosaic; after 1991 the red star and worker's red book were removed.

name: Musée National du Moudjahid
funding: A state museum created by Ordinance 66-72 of 1972, opened 5 July 1982 and under the Ministry of Mujahideen since 1993. Entry costs 20 dinars, free for mujahideen and soldiers.
watch: Beneath the Maqam Echahid esplanade, with wings on the 1830 resistance, the 1954 to 1962 war and independence; Lavalin built it to Bachir Yelles's design.

propaganda.summary: President Chadli unveiled the Maqam Echahid complex in 1982 to represent national unity and strengthen the FLN regime's legitimacy, Sarah Gray writes in Ibraaz. The museum has run under the Ministry of Mujahideen since 1993.

name: Antarctic Biennale
location: Antarctic Peninsula (shipborne; landings included Cuverville Island), Antarctica
funding: One voyage, March 2017, costing well over US$1M. Most of the money came from Eugene Kaspersky; Qiao Zhibing and Lihsin Tsai also paid, and BMW Group partnered the open call.
watch: In June 2024 the US put Kaspersky Lab on its Entity List and sanctioned twelve of its leaders; no second edition has been found.
why_flagged: Its main sponsor's company, Kaspersky Lab, was placed on the US Entity List and its leadership sanctioned by OFAC in June 2024, after the 2017 voyage.
records_note: No accounts found. Main backer named as the Oceanic Project Foundation, chaired by Anna Somers Cocks of The Art Newspaper; its old web address now serves gambling spam.

name: Australian Antarctic Arts Fellowship
funding: Run by the Australian Antarctic Division, which covers travel, meals and lodging; ANAT, assisted by Creative Australia, adds A$5,000 per fellow.
watch: Fellows may go to Casey, Davis, Mawson or Macquarie Island; the 2025 fellow worked at Casey.
records_note: The Division publishes the fellowship's terms and past fellows; no annual cost is published.

name: Esperanza Base museum
funding: A small museum inside an Argentine Army base, paid for by the Argentine state; residents show cruise visitors around it.
watch: The Army says the base exists to strengthen Argentina's sovereignty in its claimed territory; over a thousand tourists visit a year.
records_note: No museum budget is published; the Army and Foreign Ministry pages describe the base, not the museum's money.

name: Hillary's Hut (TAE/IGY Hut A), Scott Base
funding: Restored in 2016-17 by the Antarctic Heritage Trust, which raised NZ$784,000 and received a NZ$180,000 government grant in November 2016 to finish the work.
watch: It still serves as a refuge inside New Zealand's Scott Base, so most people see it through the Trust's virtual reality tour.
records_note: The Trust files audited annual returns with New Zealand's Charities Register; Antarctica New Zealand provided logistics.
